newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus to protest Turkish flights-official.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus to protest Turkish flights-official.

text.p: Cyprus will protest to the United Nations over Turkish reconnaissance flights over the island last week, an official said on Monday.

Yiannakis Cassoulides, spokesman for the Greek Cypriot-led government, confirmed reports by the semi-official media that two Turkish RF-4 planes were detected by army radars last Thursday flying around the island's south and western coast.
The Greek Cypriots are constructing military bases on the western coast under a joint defence pact the island has with Greece, its closest ally.
"It has happened before. They (the Turks) are always taking photographs and they are comparing them with the previous ones to see any changes," Cassoulides told Reuters.

The island has been divided since 1974 when Turkish forces invaded after Greek Cypriots staged a coup backed by the military regime then ruling Greece. Negotiations to unite the two communities in a federation have stalled.

Tension between the island's Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities rose last month after the Cyprus government announced plans to buy anti-aircraft missiles from Russia and Turkish threats of military action to block their deployment.

Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash said two weeks ago that people would not be moved into the abandoned resort town of Varosha in the Turkish-held areas on the eastern coast unless Greek Cypriots went ahead with their plans to buy the anti-aircraft missiles.
Denktash heads a Turkish Cypriot breakaway state in the northern third of the island. Only Ankara, which has some 30,000 troops there, recognises the breakaway state.
Turkish Cypriot ultra-nationalist leader Mehmet Arslan at the weekend called on followers to enter the empty Greek Cypriot resort and lay claim to houses there during a march to the town on March 2.
"We do not believe any of the authorities will stop us ...Anyone who likes any of the houses there should spray their name on it, that house will then be theirs," Arslan said.
Under a U.N.-brokered agreement, the town remains fenced off and uninhabited. The U.N. holds the Turkish government responsible for the maintenance of the status quo there.
Cassoulides said the situation was being monitored closely.
"Whatever happens within the fenced area of Varosha will be in flagrant violation of Security Council resolutions, for which Turkey will be solely responsible," he said.
